craft_claim: A threatened behavioral freedom produces reactance, a motivational arousal whose magnitude scales with the freedom's importance, so defiant voice persuades when it voices and restores a freedom the reader already holds rather than issuing commands.

supporting_evidence.location: A Theory of Psychological Reactance, chs. 1-2
supporting_evidence.note: Brehm establishes reactance as a motivational state aroused when a behavioral freedom is threatened or eliminated, directed at restoring the freedom; magnitude rises with the importance of the freedom.

supporting_evidence.location: Psychological Reactance: A Theory of Freedom and Control, ch. 2
supporting_evidence.note: The Brehms consolidate the four elements (perceived freedom, threat to freedom, reactance, restoration) and show that the proportion of freedoms threatened increases total reactance.
The review defines reactance as unpleasant motivational arousal at threat or loss of free behaviors and notes it can be elicited by messages and recommendations, not only by rules.
Ambedkar frames constitutional guarantees as freedoms the citizen already holds, positioning the audience as owners of rights rather than recipients of permission.

counterevidence.note: Reactance is intertwined cognition and affect directed partly at the message source, so a defiant text that commands its own audience can trigger reactance against the writer rather than the opponent.

scope: Direct-address, second-person, manifesto, and civic prose where the audience perceives the contested freedom as already theirs.
exceptions: Audiences that do not perceive the freedom as theirs (for example, a reader who identifies with the power being resisted) will not experience the same reactance restoration.
When legitimate reasons for the restriction are supplied, the threat narrows and reactance magnitude falls.
